source.title: The Consolation of Philosophy
source.description:
Boethius composed De Consolation Philosophiaein the sixth century A.D. while awaiting death by torture, condemned on a charge of plotting against Gothic rule, which he protested as manifestly unjust. Though a Christian, Boethius details the true end of life as the soul's knowledge of God, and consoles himself with the tenets of Greek philosophy, not with Christian precepts.
Written in a form called Meippean Satire that alternates between prose and verse, Boethius' work often consists of a story told by Ovid...

raw.author: Plato
contexts: Did I not often in days of old, before my servant Plato lived, wage stern warfare with the rashness of folly?

If Plato's teaching erreth not, We learn but that we have forgot.
since thou hast learnt on Plato's authority that words ought to be akin to the matter of which they treat.

From all which considerations appeareth the power of the good, and the indubitable weakness of the bad, and it is clear that Plato's judgment was true; the wise alone are able to do what they would, while the wicked follow their own hearts' lust, but can _not_ accomplish what they would.
as one more excellent than I[N] hath said: 'The very body of the holy saint Is built of purest ether.'
they deem not rightly who imagine that on Plato's principles the created world is made co-eternal with the Creator, because they are told that he believed the world to have had no beginning in time

commentaries: The author mentions Plato as a servant of Philosophy, referring to him as a historical figure and source of philosophical ideas.
The author recalls Plato's maxim about philosophers ruling or rulers becoming philosophers, attributing it to Plato himself.
The author refers to Plato's work the 'Timæus' as the source for the idea that divine protection should be invoked in all matters, even trivial ones.
The author references Plato's doctrine of reminiscence, agreeing with it.
The author invokes Plato's principle that language should be appropriate to its subject matter to justify the use of internal rather than external arguments.
The author cites Plato's judgment as a source of the idea that the wise alone can do what they will, while the wicked cannot.

The author paraphrases a line attributed to a poet or philosopher of higher insight, but the footnote indicates the source as Parmenides. However, the attribution is to a figure considered 'more excellent' than Boethius, and the footnote clarifies it is Parmenides, a pre-Socratic philosopher.
